title: You Need to be a Good Juggler to be a Good Boss (and Here's Why)
author: Gaurav Jain
summary: Jain takes the familiar leadership-versus-management dichotomy and refuses to let it stay a dichotomy. He opens with the image of a circus juggler, whose central demand is not strength but sustained attention, and argues that the good boss is doing the same thing with two different roles. He defines leadership as influence, vision and motivation independent of formal rank, and management as the operational discipline of prioritising needs, allocating resources and guaranteeing continuity. The move the piece makes is to reject the common framing that a person is either a leader or a manager: a good boss is both, and the real skill is knowing which role a given moment calls for. Jain notes from experience that he has seen as many leaders who cannot manage as managers who cannot lead, and treats the failure mode as symmetrical. He closes on the optimistic half of the analogy - juggling looks impossible to the untrained but is a learnable skill, and so is role-switching. A short piece whose value is the framing rather than any method.
points: Jain's operative claim is that leader and manager are not two kinds of person but two roles one person alternates between, so the diagnostic question is not 'which am I' but 'which does this situation need'.
He identifies the symmetrical failure mode worth watching for in yourself: leaders who never manage and managers who never lead fail in the same way, by holding only one ball in the air.
The essay pins the leadership half to influence, vision and direction-setting rather than title or rank, which makes it available to people without formal authority.

Management is given a substantive and non-dismissive definition here - determining needs, prioritising solutions, allocating resources, guaranteeing continuity of operation - rather than being treated as the lesser activity.
The closing turn is the practical one: role-switching is framed as a trainable skill rather than a temperament, so a boss who is weak on one side is not stuck there.
quotes: Leadership: What defines a leader is their influence, motivation, and vision rather than their formal rank or title. A leader will choose the course of action, inspire and involve their teams, and foster an atmosphere that encourages development and new ideas.

Management: A manager, on the other hand, is concerned with seeing that things get done. It entails determining needs, identifying possible solutions, and prioritizing those solutions to meet those needs.
So, are leaders and managers different individuals? No, they’re not. A good boss is both a leader and a manager, and knows when to assume which role.

I like to draw the analogy between a good boss and a proficient juggler. A good boss is constantly juggling between leadership and management because both of these are critical roles and essential for long-term success in any business. I have seen countless leaders who fail to manage, and countless managers who fail to lead.
And the analogy doesn’t stop there. Juggling is hard, at least for someone who hasn’t done it. But it’s a skill that’s learnable.

So, leadership and management are two complementary yet distinct roles, and really two sides of the same coin. While management provides structure and efficiency, leadership inspires and drives change.
